title: Arrhenius-Type Description and Noise-Composition Dependence of Single-Vacancy Hopping in Active Brownian Crystals
abstract: We study vacancy-mediated hopping in a two-dimensional active Brownian-particle crystal with a single vacancy. Under active driving, the hopping rates are not organized by the free-particle effective noise amplitude alone. In contrast, in the passive limit, the hopping rate follows an Arrhenius-like activated trend with respect to the translational diffusion coefficient. Effective-noise comparisons show systematic dependence on the active fraction, indicating that the composition of thermal and persistent active fluctuations affects the hopping kinetics. These results demonstrate a breakdown of an effective-temperature description for microscopic defect-mediated transport in an active crystal.
summary: This work investigates how vacancies hop through an active crystal, challenging the assumption that transport rates depend only on a total effective noise temperature. By analyzing deviations from simple models, the authors show that the specific composition of thermal versus active fluctuations dictates the hopping kinetics. This demonstrates a breakdown of the standard effective-temperature description for defect-mediated transport in driven matter.
main_problem: To determine if vacancy-mediated hopping in an active crystal is governed solely by a single effective noise amplitude or if the composition of thermal versus persistent active fluctuations matters.
main_result: The hopping kinetics cannot be described by a simple effective temperature; the rate depends systematically on the 'active fraction' ($\chi$), indicating that fluctuation composition is crucial.
method: Numerical simulation using overdamped Langevin equations to calculate long-time average hop rates, followed by fitting these rates against theoretical models based on effective noise parameters.
model_or_system: A two-dimensional active Brownian-particle (ABP) crystal containing a single vacancy. Dynamics are modeled with repulsive interactions and include both thermal diffusion ($D_t$) and persistent active driving forces.
key_observables: Hopping rate ($k$), Effective Temperature ($T_{	ext{eff}}$), Active Fraction ($\chi$), and the deviation residual ($\delta \ln k$).
important_parameters: Active fraction ($\chi$), translational diffusion coefficient ($D_t$), and the comparison to the passive limit.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the hopping-solid-like state, and the derived equations are effective descriptions over specific parameter regimes.
figures_summary: Figure 2(a) shows passive rates following an Arrhenius law. Figure 2(b) demonstrates that active rates do not collapse onto a single curve when plotted against $1/T_{	ext{eff}}$, showing systematic deviations organized by $\chi$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the baseline using the passive limit (Arrhenius behavior). It then compares active hopping rates to predictions based only on $T_{	ext{eff}}$, revealing discrepancies. Finally, it develops a phenomenological model incorporating the active fraction ($\chi$) to explain these systematic deviations.
why_interesting: The breakdown of simple effective-temperature descriptions in driven systems is highly relevant for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex quantum or classical many-body systems where noise sources are heterogeneous.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

(b) Effective-noise test: even using Teff = Dt + a2Pe2 r/2, active and passive data do not fall on a single curve versus 1/Teff. Error bars denote two-sided 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals over independent runs.

Figure 3: (Color online) Noise-composition dependence beyond a scalar effective-noise de- scription. The passive-normalized residual δ ln k is plotted against the active fraction χ = (a2Pe2 r/2)/Teff. Color indicates Teff. Panel (a) shows all retained hopping-solid-like state points, whereas panel (b) focuses on the low-effective-noise subset Teff < 0.5. The solid line in panel (b) is a weighted linear fit to this subset, and the dashed line denotes zero residual.
